I’m 64 years old, a white woman who has spent the last few decades navigating life with a visual impairment and a chronic condition called multiple chemical sensitivity. I earned my bachelor’s degree in communications from a local university in the early 1980s, and that education has helped me stay connected to the world even when my sight is limited. I don’t drive; I don’t have a driver’s license, and I don’t own a car. Instead, I rely on taxis or limousines to get to work and on public transit for most of my daily travel. I take public transit at least five times a week, even though I don’t have a vehicle that can accompany me on those trips.

I’ve lived in my current apartment for just over a year, renting the place in a neighborhood that’s close to the bus stops and subway lines I use. I’m employed part‑time, working about 15 hours a week in a gig‑based role that doesn’t have a fixed workplace. I’m a freelance event coordinator and occasional informal tutor, moving from venue to venue or from client to client each week. Because I don’t have a permanent office, I often work in coffee shops, community centers, or clients’ homes. My job requires me to be flexible and to travel frequently, which is why I rely on public transit and taxis to get where I need to be.

Living with multiple chemical sensitivity means I’m very careful about the environments I enter. I avoid places with strong fumes, harsh cleaning products, or any chemicals that could trigger an allergic reaction. That sensitivity also makes it harder to work in traditional office settings, so the freelance nature of my work is a blessing. I can choose the venues that are safe and comfortable for me.

I’m not married, and I don’t have children. I’m proud of my independence and the way I’ve adapted to my circumstances. Even though I’m 64 and still working, I feel young at heart. I’ve learned that staying active, staying connected, and staying true to my own needs is the best way to keep going.

I’m Maya, a 21‑year‑old full‑time student at Central City Community College, working toward an associate degree in health sciences. I grew up in a multiracial household—my mother is of Latino descent, my father has African‑American and Asian roots—and I’ve lived in the same four‑bedroom house on Oak Street for the past 23 years. My parents are the primary household respondents, and I’m their daughter who now shares the mortgage on our home, paying about $1,200 a month on a 30‑year loan.

I’m a personal care assistant by trade, a role that fits my passion for helping others and my schedule. I work 16 hours a week, split over two days, and I don’t have a fixed workplace. Instead, I travel to different clients’ homes in a car as a passenger—my friend drives, and I hop in. Because I don’t have a driver’s license, I rely on public transit for most of my commute to school and for the occasional ride to a client’s house when I can’t find a ride share. I use the bus or the subway at least five times a week, and I never have a vehicle available when I’m on public transit.

Living with diabetes is part of my everyday life. I monitor my blood sugar with a glucometer before meals, after meals, and before bed. I schedule insulin injections around my classes and work shifts, and I always carry a snack in my backpack in case my glucose dips. My condition does limit my daily travel in subtle ways—I have to plan routes that allow me to pause for a quick check, and I’m careful about the timing of my meals and medication. Still, I manage it well enough to keep up with my coursework and part‑time job.

I’m proud to be a homeowner at 21, a student, and a part‑time caregiver. My life is a balancing act of school, work, health, and family, but I keep moving forward—whether that’s riding the bus to the community college, driving as a passenger to a client’s home, or staying at home to prepare for the next day.

I was born in 1933 in a small farming town in Illinois, the eldest of three children. My parents ran a modest grocery store, and I spent my early years helping out on the shelves and learning to read the weather by the wind in the fields. From a young age, I noticed that I couldn't hear as well as my siblings; my hearing impairment made conversations a bit of a puzzle, but I learned to listen to the rustle of leaves and the hum of the radio to keep in tune with the world.

After high school, I attended a local community college on a part‑time basis while raising my own family. I earned a handful of college credits—mostly in history and English—but never finished a degree. Education was always a passion, even if it never led to a diploma on my transcript.

I never held a job outside the home. My husband worked as a machinist at the nearby factory, and I took care of our house, our three children, and later, our grandchildren. Even after retirement, I stayed at home, managing the household and keeping the family’s traditions alive. I never had a driver’s license, and I have always relied on public transit or family members for transportation. My home, which I bought with a mortgage in 1965, has been my sanctuary for 58 years; the walls have seen my children grow up, the house has survived a few harsh winters, and the garden in the back has been a place of quiet reflection.

Living with a hearing impairment and a mental and emotional disability has shaped much of my daily routine. I use a cane or walker for short distances, and I have a transferable wheelchair for longer trips. My disability limits my daily travel—most of my outings are short, close to home, and often accompanied by my daughter or a friend. I don’t drive, so I have no vehicle available when using public transit, and I rarely, if ever, take the bus to work because I’m no longer employed.

I am the mother of the primary respondent in this survey. Watching my daughter grow into a woman and a mother herself has been my greatest pride. My days are filled with the quiet sounds of my garden, the occasional call from my grandchildren, and the soft music that I used to listen to on the radio. I am a white woman, not Hispanic, and I cherish the simple, steady rhythm of my life, even as the world around me changes.

I’m the older brother in my household, and we’ve lived in the house I own with a mortgage for the past year. I’m the one who keeps the lights on and the fridge stocked, and I’m always ready to help my sister or cousin with homework or household chores.

Because my disability doesn’t limit my daily travel, I can move around the neighborhood without a cane or walker. I never use public transit to get to work, and I don’t have a toll payment method—my life is pretty simple. I love the rhythm of my routine: a quick walk to the store, a few hours of cooking and serving, and then back home to study, practice my Spanish, and plan for the next week. My life is a mix of hard work, learning, and family, and I wouldn’t trade it for anything.

I was born blind, and I’ve been deaf since childhood. I navigate the world with a white cane and a motorized wheelchair that’s designed for transfers—so I can get on and off it with a little help. I also use a walker for extra stability when I’m on uneven surfaces. In addition to these physical disabilities, I have a mental health condition that sometimes makes it hard to focus for long periods, which affects my daily routine and limits how far I can travel.

I don’t use a car regularly, but I do have access to a vehicle that I can use when I need to travel longer distances—usually a friend or family member will drive me. I can’t get around on my own, so I plan my trips carefully and often use a combination of bus rides and rideshares. My mobility limitations mean I’m cautious about how many miles I cover each day, and I often schedule errands and appointments close to my home.

I’m not currently enrolled in school or a training program, and I don’t volunteer on a regular basis—though I’ve helped out at the local community center on a few occasions when I can. I was born in 1924 in a small town in Alabama and grew up in a close‑knit African‑American community. After high school, I earned a scholarship to Howard University, where I completed a bachelor’s degree in Sociology in 1946 and went on to earn a Ph.D. in Social Work in 1952. I spent the next three decades as a professor of social work at a community college in Washington, D.C., mentoring countless students and conducting research on urban poverty and family dynamics. I retired in 2000, after 30 years of teaching and community service.

In 2008, I moved to my current home in a quiet suburban neighborhood in Maryland. I’ve lived there for the past 15 years, and it’s the place where my family and I have celebrated birthdays, holidays, and the milestones of my grandchildren. I own the house outright and have taken pride in keeping it well maintained, despite the challenges I face.

I’m 99 years old now, a proud African‑American male who has seen so many changes in the world. I am the father of my daughter, who is now a high‑school senior, and the grandfather of a 13‑year‑old son who is preparing for his freshman year. I still keep in touch with my daughter’s friends and my grandson’s teachers, often through phone calls or video chats, even though I’m both visually and hearing impaired. I use a cane for mobility and a walker for longer distances. Because of my disabilities, I’m unable to drive and I don’t have a driver’s license. I also don’t own a vehicle, so I rely on public transit for any trips that I must make, although my travel is limited to essential errands and visits to my doctor’s office.

I am no longer employed; I’m retired and spend most of my days reading, listening to music on a screen‑reader, and keeping up with my family’s lives. I don’t volunteer regularly, and I don’t have any formal education enrollment at the moment. I don’t travel to work—my work was in the past—and I don’t have any current employer. I also don’t use toll payment methods or have any other transportation arrangements beyond the public transit system.

Despite the challenges that my visual and hearing impairments present, I find joy in the simple moments: watching the sunrise from my porch, hearing my grandson’s laughter as he plays video games, and feeling the rhythm of my cane as I walk to the mailbox. My life has been shaped by perseverance, faith, and the love of my family.
